courses.description: This course is designed to explore the principles and practices of effective leadership within the context of Recreation Management. Students will examine various leadership theories, models, and styles, with a focus on their application in recreational settings. Emphasis will be placed on developing essential leadership skills, including communication, decision-making, team building, conflict resolution, and strategic planning. The leadership concepts and skills learned in this course would be beneficial in any other field.

courses.title: Inclusion and Disabilities in Therapeutic Recreation
courses.description:
This course explores the intersection of recreation, accessibility, and inclusion. As future recreation professionals, students will gain essential knowledge and skills to create welcoming and equitable recreational environments for all individuals, including those with disabilities. The course delves into legal frameworks, societal attitudes, historical context, and practical strategies to foster inclusive spaces. By the end of this course, students will be prepared to advocate for accessibility, challenge stereotypes, and promote a sense of belonging in recreational settings. 

Note: Students are required to obtain practicum hours for the course; it is highly recommended to register for RM 240L, as this lab opportunity will help students obtain the required practicum hours. Students may obtain alternate practicum hours through an approval process.

courses.title: Outdoor Leadership Seminar
courses.description: This course is designed as a practicum of many core elements of the recreation management program in an event management environment.  Students will utilize concepts of program management, event logistics, budgeting, leadership, risk management, expedition group care, and hospitality.  Implementation of a wide range of outdoor event skills such as backpacking, orienteering, stargazing, canoeing, mountain biking, cross-country skiing,  snowshoeing, winter camping, primitive skills, and other appropriate seasonal activities will be learned, practiced, and taught by each student.  This course will introduce students to environments similar to many common commercial or municipal outdoor recreation providers as an effort to prepare them for careers in the outdoor industry.

courses.title: Wilderness First Aid
courses.description: This course provides students with the knowledge and skills necessary to respond to medical emergencies in wilderness and remote settings. Emphasizing hands-on learning and practical scenarios, students may gain a Wilderness First Aid certification, CPR/AED certification, and develop the confidence to address injuries and illnesses when traditional emergency services are not readily available. The course covers patient assessment, common wilderness injuries and illnesses, medical decision-making, and essential survival skills. There may be one overnight or late-night field trip during the semester to engage in a mock First Aid activity.

courses.title: Backpacking
courses.description: This course immerses students in the fundamental skills and knowledge required for safe and enjoyable backpacking experiences. From navigation and equipment use to environmental awareness and group dynamics, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of the backpacking experience. Emphasis is placed on developing technical skills, fostering environmental stewardship, and promoting personal wellness through outdoor activities.

courses.title: Traditional Camping
courses.description: This intermediate course provides skills, training, and theory of historical traditional camping as well as leadership development through the medium of traditional camping skills and ideals. This course focuses on simple, minimum impact technology, and mastery of technique. Skills will be land-based and relate directly to the environment in which they are taught. The course also has a strong academic component requiring reading, writing, and critical thinking skills as needed to address case studies and contemporary issues in the field of Outdoor/Adventure Education. A three-day trip is required where students will use the skills learned.

courses.title: Survival
courses.description: This is an introductory course in basic earth skills and survival philosophy. Instruction will include, but is not limited to, finding water, primitive fire building, shelter construction, use of natural fibers, fishing, primitive tool weapons, and stone working. A three-day trip is required where students will use the skills learned.

courses.title: Mountain Biking
courses.description: This introductory course includes mountain bike riding techniques, skills, conditioning, and maintenance. Group management and leadership will also be emphasized.  The course involves weekly 10 to 20 mile rides with different levels of difficulty. Students must provide or rent their own bikes. Skills acquired in this class can aid students who desire to work as guides or Outdoor Recreation Specialists.  This course requires mandatory Field Experiences.  Instructors will contact students with trip information prior to the start of the semester.

courses.title: Rock Climbing
courses.description: This course is designed to introduce students to movement on rock, equipment, knots and hitches, belaying technique, and protection and anchoring. Students will develop proficiencies in safe climbing site management and will increase their teaching and leadership skills.  This course requires mandatory Field Experiences.  Instructors will contact students with trip information prior to the start of the semester.

courses.title: Mountaineering
courses.description: This course provides students with the skills needed for traveling through third, fourth, and fifth class mountainous terrain, navigation and route finding, pace management, small team rescue, self-arrests, and snow anchor techniques. Students will also refine rock climbing, protection and anchoring skills, and apply these techniques to mountain settings. Emphasis will be placed on student leadership, teaching development, group, and risk management.  This course requires mandatory Field Experiences.  Instructors will contact students with trip information prior to the start of the semester.

courses.title: Outdoor Cooking
courses.description: This introductory course utilizes multiple outdoor cooking techniques and offers an opportunity for students to appreciate the beautiful outdoor surroundings of Eastern Idaho. Students will learn safe and sanitary practices. Students will utilize and create multiple types of cooking equipment. Working together in groups and individually, students will menu plan, prepare food, and participate in an overnight camp trip. To be an effective outdoor cook, working in a team is vital. Extensive group work is required in this course. This class is held outdoors no matter the weather conditions; you are required to provide your own personal camping gear and clothing attire for this course.

courses.title: Canyoneering
courses.description: This course develops skills in decision-making for safely managing groups in a technical canyon environment. Additional topics include equipment selection and use, rappelling technique, knot tying, anchor evaluation and construction, canyon rescue, and risk evaluation. It requires mandatory Field Experiences.  Instructors will contact students with trip information before the start of the semester.

courses.title: Fly Tying
courses.description: This course immerses students in the art and craft of fly tying, focusing on developing skills, knowledge, and appreciation for the tradition of creating fishing flies. From mastering basic patterns to exploring entomology and expressing creativity, students will gain hands-on experience in a variety of fly-tying techniques.

courses.title: Canoeing
courses.description: This introductory course includes instruction on flat and moving water (Class 1 and 2). Students will learn the various paddle strokes, rescue techniques, canoe packing, trip management skills, and equipment selection and use.  This course requires mandatory Field Experiences.  Instructors will contact students with trip information prior to the start of the semester.

courses.title: Cross Country Skiing
courses.description: This introductory course (no previous experience required) includes instruction on winter clothing equipment, and basic classic Nordic skiing techniques. Each class session will be in snow, often in a back country setting. Students will learn techniques including the diagonal stride, double polling, side stepping, the herringbone, and wedge. This course also focuses on outdoor trip planning and teaching skills,  group management, and expedition behavior in a winter environment. Students will be required to participate weekly in mandatory Field Experiences. Instructors will contact students with trip information prior to the start of the semester.

courses.title: Winter Outdoor Skills
courses.description: This course will require students to develop leadership and skills to lead groups in harsh cold weather conditions. Students will learn about proper winter clothing, cooking, travel techniques, safety, and environmental awareness. Students will stay in either tents or snow shelters of their own making. This course requires mandatory Field Experiences. Instructors will contact students with trip information before the start of the semester.

courses.title: Backcountry Ski Touring
courses.description: This course is purely experiential in nature by having students spend the day in the winter back country learning safe travel either on Telemark skis, Alpine touring skis, or split board snowboards. Specific topics covered include group leadership and management, avalanche awareness, ski and snowboard skills in powder snow, route finding, and search and rescue. Students must supply their own skis or snowboard, or rent from the ORC.  This course requires mandatory Field Experiences.  Instructors will contact students with trip information prior to the start of the semester.

courses.title: Therapeutic Recreation Lab
courses.description: This lab allows students to practice hands-on skills in Therapeutic Recreation programs on and off campus.  Hours in the program count for practicum hours needed in the other therapeutic recreation classes, which may be taken concurrently.

courses.title: Introduction to Therapeutic Recreation
courses.description:
In this course students will explore the dynamic field of Therapeutic Recreation. Through comprehensive study, they will gain a deep understanding of the role of recreation and leisure in enhancing well-being and quality of life. Students will become familiar with essential terminology and foundational concepts related to Therapeutic Recreation. They will delve into the Therapeutic Recreation process, covering assessment, planning, implementation, and evaluation. By examining how recreational activities contribute to positive outcomes, students will appreciate the impact of tailored interventions. Additionally, they will identify diverse client populations that benefit from Therapeutic Recreation and learn strategies for selecting appropriate leisure activities. As they explore career paths within the field, students will recognize the importance of ongoing professional growth.  This course is required for students specializing in Therapeutic Recreation and professionals who wish to work in fields such as healthcare and social services. 

Note: Students are required to obtain practicum hours for the course; it is highly recommended to register for RM 366L or RM 373, as these provide opportunities that will help students obtain the required practicum hours. Students may obtain the required practicum hours through an approval process. Course modalities are offered on an alternating schedule. Consult with the department to plan according to the student's preferred modality.

courses.title: Family Recreation
courses.description: This Family Recreation course explores the dynamics of recreation within the family environment, equipping students with the tools necessary to implement principles for successful and ethical family-focused recreational practices. Emphasizing gospel values set forth by the Living Prophets, students will delve into the multifaceted aspects of family life, recreation, and social sciences. Suitable for those entering professions related to family life, recreation, and social sciences, this course provides a holistic understanding of how recreational activities can positively impact eternal families, family dynamics, and overall well-being.

courses.title: Leisure in Society
courses.description: This course serves as an engaging introduction to the foundational theories, philosophies, concepts, and historical perspectives that shape the field of Recreation Management. Delve into the challenges associated with leisure, explore core leisure values, and analyze the profound impact that leisure has on individuals, families, and society. Gain a comprehensive understanding of how leisure contributes to spiritual well-being, mental well-being, physical well-being, social well-being, and community dynamics. Through thoughtful examination and practical applications, students will develop a nuanced perspective on the vital role of leisure in shaping our lives and society.

courses.title: Program and Event Management
courses.description: This course is designed to equip students with essential organizational and administrative skills crucial for effective planning and development of recreation programs. With a strong emphasis on theoretical concepts and practical applications, students will delve into the intricacies of program and event planning across commercial, public, and non-profit settings. Tailored for entry-level professionals aspiring to work in any facet of the recreation field, this course offers a comprehensive understanding of the skills required to design and execute successful programs in diverse recreational environments.

courses.title: Outdoor Recreation Management and Ethics
courses.description: Explore the dynamic intersection of outdoor recreation, management, and ethical stewardship in this upper-division course designed for upper-division students aspiring to leadership roles within the outdoor recreation industry. This course combines theoretical knowledge with practical skills, equipping students with the expertise needed to navigate the complexities of outdoor recreation administration while instilling a strong ethical foundation. Engage in critical discussions, case studies, and hands-on activities to develop the competencies necessary for effective leadership in the diverse and evolving field of outdoor recreation. Embrace the responsibility of shaping sustainable and responsible practices within the industry, preparing for impactful roles in the management of outdoor recreation.

courses.title: Introduction to Sport Management
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the principles, theories, and practices of sport management. Topics covered include the history and evolution of sport management, organizational structures in sport, leadership and decision-making, marketing and promotions, financial management, legal issues, ethics, and current trends in the sport industry.

courses.title: Commercial Recreation
courses.description: This course offers students an in-depth exploration of the history, characteristics, and management aspects of commercial recreation within the dynamic field of leisure and recreation. With a primary focus on entrepreneurship and small business operations, students will delve into case study analysis and field investigation methods, actively participating in the learning process. A key highlight of the course is the creation and management of a commercial recreation business, providing hands-on experience in applying marketing techniques, budgeting, and other essential management principles.

courses.title: Environmental Interpretation
courses.description:
In this course, students will examine the historical foundations and theoretical frameworks of interpretation through a gospel-centered lens while recognizing that “all things denote there is a God” and the role of stewardship for God’s creations. Through a blend of theoretical study and practical application, students will learn to design and implement interpretive programs that create meaningful connections between audiences and natural resources.

Students will develop interpretive lessons using cognitive learning theory, the T.O.R.E. Model, and strategies that provoke thought and advance the understanding of our natural and cultural heritage. Hands-on experiences will teach you how to engage diverse audiences, inspire stewardship, and cultivate a deeper appreciation for the world as a divine creation. Participants will gain critical skills in creating engaging, theme-based interpretive products suitable for various settings, including parks, museums, and other natural and environmental settings and programs.

courses.title: Experiential Education
courses.description: This intermediate-level course delves into the principles and practices of designing and facilitating experiential learning activities. Students will develop leadership and team-building skills through hands-on applications in diverse settings. The course emphasizes the exploration of alternative facilitation techniques, providing students with a versatile toolkit for effective experiential education. Open to all recreation majors, as well as students in education and the social sciences, this course offers a dynamic exploration of experiential learning methods applicable across various professional domains.

courses.title: Adaptive Recreation in Therapeutic Recreation
courses.description: This course provides students with knowledge and skills needed to meet the unique fitness and physical activity needs of individuals with various disabilities. The principles and techniques learned in this course may be applied in multiple settings, including clinical and community. Through class discussions, course assignments, and a service learning experience, students will learn how to apply the principles of Therapeutic Recreation to design and implement disability sports/recreation programs for individuals with disabilities based on assessments of health-related strengths and needs.

courses.title: Therapeutic Recreation: Evidence Practice
courses.description: This required course delves into the foundations of therapeutic recreation, exploring various practice models and interdisciplinary theories. Students will gain a deep understanding of evidence-based practice in therapeutic recreation programming, learning to develop specific programs through a rigorous process. The course emphasizes substantial group work, ensuring students' engagement in collaborative learning. Additionally, periodic in-person meetings with the instructor are integral, fostering meaningful interactions in face-to-face, virtual, and online modalities.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RM212 - Inclusion and Disabilities in Therapeutic Recreation (3) ; RM270 - Introduction to Therapeutic Recreation (3)

courses.title: Applied Therapeutic Recreation
courses.description: This course, tailored for Therapeutic Recreation students, offers a comprehensive exploration of evidence-based practice in real-world settings. Students will gain valuable work experience with applicable populations, focusing on the practical implementation of the Therapeutic Recreation (TR) Process. The TR Process encompasses Assessment, Planning, Intervention, Evaluation, and Documentation. Throughout the course, students will actively design treatment plans, evaluate the benefits of therapeutic interventions for specific populations, and employ a range of evidence-based practices. This immersive experience prepares students for the dynamic challenges of applying evidence-based principles in therapeutic recreation.

courses.title: Therapeutic Recreation: Assessment and Evaluation
courses.description: This course focuses on patient assessment including quantitative and qualitative date, treatment plan development, and evaluation. Students will be required to apply these skills from the Therapeutic Recreation Process in a variety of settings. This is a required course for all students within Therapeutic Recreation. Due to the nature of this profession, substantial group work is required; in addition, periodic in person meetings with the instructor will occur; this applies to face to face, virtual and online modalities.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RM371 - Therapeutic Recreation: Evidence Practice (3) ; RM270 - Introduction to Therapeutic Recreation (3)

courses.title: Therapeutic Recreation: Program Dynamic
courses.description:
This required course in Therapeutic Recreation offers students practical exposure to a diverse range of therapeutic techniques, aiming to develop clinical skills and competencies essential for planning and implementing programs for individuals with disabilities. Through active application of skills within the Therapeutic Recreation process across varied settings, students will gain hands-on experience. The course is designed to be a cornerstone for students with an emphasis in Therapeutic Recreation, providing them with a comprehensive understanding of programming dynamics.

Note: The incorporation of substantial group work fosters collaborative learning, reflecting the interactive nature of the therapeutic recreation profession. Furthermore, periodic in-person meetings with the instructor ensure meaningful engagement in face-to-face, virtual, and online modalities.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RM270 - Introduction to Therapeutic Recreation (3) ; RM371 - Therapeutic Recreation: Evidence Practice (3)

courses.title: Therapeutic Recreation: Advancement of the Profession
courses.description:
This required course in Therapeutic Recreation lays the foundation for addressing crucial issues related to professional competence, financial management, and supervisory communication within the field. Students will explore advanced concepts essential for the progression of therapeutic recreation as a profession. The course is specifically designed for students majoring in Therapeutic Recreation, offering insights into the practical aspects of financial management and effective supervisory communication. 

NOTE: Substantial group work is incorporated to foster collaborative learning and periodic in-person meetings with the instructor are facilitated, ensuring meaningful engagement in face-to-face, virtual, and online modalities.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RM270 - Introduction to Therapeutic Recreation (3) ; RM371 - Therapeutic Recreation: Evidence Practice (3)

courses.title: Venue Management in Recreation
courses.description: This is a broad survey course of recreation facilities that helps students gain an understanding of recreation facility design and management.  A broad selection of facilities will be explored such as community centers, athletic centers, stadiums, outdoor facilities, spas, arenas, etc.  Theories and concepts that apply to the management and design of recreation facilities will be explored.

courses.title: Managing Risk in Recreation
courses.description: This comprehensive course in Recreation Management provides students with an in-depth study on effectively managing risk within the recreation profession. Students will explore the intricacies of accident occurrence, preventive measures, and lessons learned from incidents. The course also delves into the legal aspects influencing the recreation industry, emphasizing professional responsibility in the development of robust risk management protocols and procedures. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the knowledge and skills necessary to navigate and mitigate risks inherent in recreational activities.

courses.title: Research and Evaluation
courses.description: This  senior level course teaches students how to design, collect, analyze, interpret, and report information for organization/program needs assessment and evaluation. Students must complete Social Statistics (Math 221) before or while taking this course.  A semester long individual research project will be required.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take 1 of the following courses: ; MATH221A - Business Statistics (3) ; MATH221B - Biostatistics (3) ; MATH221C - Social Science Statistics (3) ; MATH221D - Introductory Statistics with R (3) ; MATH325 - Intermediate Statistics (3)

courses.title: Recreation Management Senior Internship
courses.description:
Internship credits are exempt from tuition charges. However, an administrative fee equal to one credit hour at the current rate of tuition will be charged for an internship course. The fee is in addition to any tuition charges for other classes. Fees are charged independently of tuition and are not subject to the 12-credit tuition cap.

This course requires professional-level experience in a department-approved leisure service organization and is completed near the end of the degree. Prerequisites include the completion of 24 recreation core credits and 400 hours of professional field experience. Students must contact the Recreation Internship Coordinator when planning and registering for their internship experience.

courses.title: Therapeutic Recreation Senior Internship
courses.description:
Internship credits are exempt from tuition charges. However, an administrative fee equal to one credit hour at the current rate of tuition will be charged for an internship course. The fee is in addition to any tuition charges for other classes. Fees are charged independently of tuition and are not subject to the 12-credit tuition cap.

This culminating course in Therapeutic Recreation aligns with the National Council on Therapeutic Recreation Certification (NCTRC) requirements, mandating a comprehensive 560-hour (14 consecutive weeks) internship in therapeutic recreation services. The internship emphasizes the application of the therapeutic recreation process, as defined by the current NCTRC Job Analysis Study. 

Under the joint supervision of academic and agency field placement supervisors, both NCTRC CTRS certified, students engage in real-world, hands-on experiences that prepare them for professional practice. With a commitment of at least 20 hours per week and no more than 45 hours per week, students work under the guidance of a primary supervisor, ensuring a substantial focus on therapeutic recreation services. 

The primary supervisor must dedicate a minimum of 20 hours per week to the agency, with 50% of their duties directly related to therapeutic recreation services. As a crucial step in professional development, students are required to contact the Therapeutic Recreation Internship Coordinator when planning and registering for their internship experience.

courses.title: Research and Leadership Seminar
courses.description: This course provides special intensive exposure to a selected topic in the recreation profession. The approved topic must be supervised by an assigned department faculty member.

courses.title: Beginning Russian I
courses.description: This course involves the development of the four basic language skills: speaking, listening, reading, and writing in Russian.  It is designed for beginners and students with less than two years of high school Russian.

courses.title: Beginning Russian II
courses.description: Further acquisition of basic language skills in Russian: reading, speaking, listening, and writing.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RUSS101 - Beginning Russian I (4)

courses.title: Intermediate Russian I
courses.description: Further acquisition of basic language skills in Russian: reading, speaking, listening, and writing.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RUSS102 - Beginning Russian II (4)

courses.title: Intermediate Russian II
courses.description: Analysis of level-appropriate texts in Russian, accompanied by study of intermediate-level Russian grammar. Note: This is the appropriate starting point for Russian-speaking returned missionaries.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RUSS201 - Intermediate Russian I (4)

courses.title: Advanced Russian I
courses.description: This course consists of a systematic focus on grammar, listening, speaking, writing, and reading in Russian.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RUSS202 - Intermediate Russian II (4)

courses.title: Advanced Russian II
courses.description: This course consists of a systematic focus on grammar, listening, speaking, writing, and reading in Russian.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RUSS202 - Intermediate Russian II (4)

courses.title: Russian Culture
courses.description: This course is an introduction to Russian culture, literature, art, music, and history. Taught in English.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; ENG150 - Writing and Reasoning Foundations (3)

courses.title: Russian Teaching Methods
courses.description: This course consists of developing Russian teaching skills and theories of second language acquisition.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RUSS202 - Intermediate Russian II (4)

courses.title: Independent Study in Russian
courses.description: This course consists of independent projects monitored through periodic conferences and assessments by instructor.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; RUSS202 - Intermediate Russian II (4)

courses.title: Science Teaching Principles
courses.description:
This course introduces readings on science planning, teaching, principles, theories, and standards. Students learn these concepts in conjunction with inquiry-based science teaching strategies and frameworks. They also develop several inquiry-based lesson plans based on Idaho science standards and practices. 

This course includes an early practicum component where students are expected to observe and work on a regular basis with a mentor science teacher in the public schools. 

As an introductory course, it helps the students understand the history and nature of science, as well as general principles of science teaching. This course is designed for secondary education majors seeking a science-based 6-12 teaching endorsement, and as a foundation to prepare these students for the senior-level science teaching methods and field experience course.
courses.prerequisiteText: Complete all of the following ; Take the following course(s): ; EDCOR200 - Teaching as a Profession (2) ; Take 1 of the following courses: ; BIO181 - Introduction to Biology II (3) ; CHEM106 - General Chemistry II (3) ; GEOL112 - Historical Geology (4) ; PH123 - Principles of Physics II (3)

courses.title: Integrated Science
courses.description: The main objective of this course is to gain a solid foundation on content in Biology, Physical Science, Earth and Space Science, so students can be confident in teaching these concepts in elementary school classes.  Students will learn basic concepts and principles of science and hands-on applications to aid in teaching elementary school level science activities.

courses.title: Lab Teaching Methods
courses.description: This is a comprehensive laboratory course designed specifically for biology education majors in order to familiarize them with essential laboratory techniques and equipment used in teaching high school honors, AP, and college biology. Cellular biology, molecular biology, genetics, and biochemistry will be the focus of the content of the labs learned in this class. Students will also learn about developing labs and writing lab reports at the high school level as well as becoming certified in laboratory safety.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SCIED205 - Science Teaching Principles (2)

courses.title: Science Teaching Methods
courses.description: The focus of this course is on preparing students to be in general science teaching methods and will include basic information and variances found within the different science teaching fields (i.e. Life Science, Earth Science, and Physical Science). The scope will include laboratory safety and design, incorporating demonstrations in teaching, designing curricula and assessments specific to science courses, the Next Generation Science Standards, and other teaching methods specific to science subjects. There is a practicum component to the course that will allow the students to practice these methods by teaching students at the junior high level.
courses.prerequisiteText: Complete all of the following ; Take 1 of the following courses: ; SCIED205 - Science Teaching Principles (2) ; PH 305 (last offered 2021) ; CHEM 305 (last offered 2019) ; GEOL 305 (last offered 2019)

courses.title: Middle School Science Teaching Methods
courses.description: This course covers foundational concepts of secondary education science planning, teaching, principles, theories, and standards. Students gain a foundational understanding of inquiry-based science teaching strategies and frameworks in preparation for science teaching at the middle school level. It includes basic information and variances found within the different science teaching fields (i.e., Life Science, Earth Science, and Physical Science). This is a capstone course and helps the students understand the history and nature of science, as well as general principles of science teaching. The scope includes laboratory safety and design, incorporating demonstrations in teaching, designing curricula and assessments specific to science courses, learning by inquiry, the Next Generation Science Standards, STEM-based learning, technology use in science teaching, and other teaching methods specific to science subjects. Part of this course involves a practicum that provides the students with the opportunity to practice science teaching methods and planning skills by teaching students at both the junior high level and high school levels. Students will be expected to create lesson plans based on best practices in teaching science by inquiry and through the nature of science. The practicum will also involve opportunities to interact with students at the secondary level in various science courses. A proof of performance, required for certification, will be a part of this experience.
courses.corequisiteText: Completed or concurrently enrolled in: ; ED406 - STEM Methods (2)

courses.title: Operations Management
courses.description: This course focuses on operations management principles and spreadsheet modeling skills. Topics include process strategy, productivity, quality management, project management, forecasting, inventory management, production planning, material requirements, lean production, and logistics management. Students develop skills through readings, problems, assessments, and simulations.

courses.title: Business Supply Chain Internship
courses.description:
Internship credits are exempt from tuition charges. However, an administrative fee equal to one credit hour at the current rate of tuition will be charged for an internship course. The fee is in addition to any tuition charges for other classes. Fees are charged independently of tuition and are not subject to the 12-credit tuition cap.

Required for all Supply Chain Management students. Students must be registered for this course within the first two weeks of the semester they are completing the internship. Students will find a professional  internship in an approved business, complete the application and obtain approval through the College of Business and Communication Career Services, be enrolled in the course, write reports, and submit evaluations.  During their internship students will gain a greater vision of becoming a business professional and establish career networking links. Students will earn one credit and may receive compensation from the employer and letters of recommendation from both the employer and BYU-Idaho.

courses.title: Special Topics in Operations Management
courses.description: An arranged research or special project course. Contact the department for registration information.

courses.title: Advanced Topics in Operations Management
courses.description: Explore various advanced topics in operations management.  Review basic concepts and calculations for forecasting, inventory management, ordering, project management, statistical quality management, and other operations management sub-functions.  Building upon these fundamentals, demonstrate how forecasting, planning, inventory, and ordering decisions can help an organization to effectively align supply availability with uncertain levels of demand.
courses.prerequisiteText: Complete all of the following ; Take the following course(s): ; SCM361 - Operations Management (3) ; Take 1 of the following courses: ; BA215 - Spreadsheet Analysis for Business (3) ; ME142 - Engineering Computation (3) ; Take 1 of the following courses: ; DS150 - Data Intuition and Insight (2) ; MATH221A - Business Statistics (3) ; MATH221B - Biostatistics (3) ; MATH221C - Social Science Statistics (3) ; MATH221D - Introductory Statistics with R (3) ; MATH330 - Engineering Statistics (3)

courses.title: Global Sourcing
courses.description: The course focuses on the "sourcing" aspects of supply chain management. Students learn through case studies, scholarly articles, mini-projects, current events, and interactions with supply chain professionals. Focus topics include strategic sourcing, source to settle/procure to pay process model, supplier selection, supplier relationship management, bids and proposals, negotiation, and current sourcing topics.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SCM361 - Operations Management (3)

courses.title: Logistics Management
courses.description: Students will learn problem solving, decision making, and optimization skills related to inventory management, inbound and outbound logistics, and warehouse management.
courses.prerequisiteText: Complete all of the following ; Take the following course(s): ; SCM361 - Operations Management (3) ; Take 1 of the following courses: ; DS150 - Data Intuition and Insight (2) ; MATH221A - Business Statistics (3) ; MATH221B - Biostatistics (3) ; MATH221C - Social Science Statistics (3) ; MATH221D - Introductory Statistics with R (3) ; MATH330 - Engineering Statistics (3)

courses.title: Operations Analysis and Modeling
courses.description: This course is focused on the use of computer tools and modeling techniques to support business operations analysis and decision-making.  The ability to collect, organize, interpret, and effectively communicate the relevant information is an important skill that is much needed to support business operations.  This course will give students the opportunity to strengthen these skills using a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet application.  Particular attention will be given to advanced spreadsheet capabilities, including some programming with Visual Basic for Applications (VBA).
courses.prerequisiteText: Complete all of the following ; Take the following course(s): ; SCM361 - Operations Management (3) ; Take 1 of the following courses: ; BA215 - Spreadsheet Analysis for Business (3) ; ME142 - Engineering Computation (3) ; Take 1 of the following courses: ; DS150 - Data Intuition and Insight (2) ; MATH221A - Business Statistics (3) ; MATH221B - Biostatistics (3) ; MATH221C - Social Science Statistics (3) ; MATH221D - Introductory Statistics with R (3) ; MATH330 - Engineering Statistics (3)

courses.title: Introduction to Sociology
courses.description: This course focuses on the social and cultural foundations of human life.  Its basic concepts enable the students to better appreciate how they and others are molded and shaped by society, and to understand the complexity of the social forces in their environment.

courses.title: Skills in Social Competence: How to Know a Person
courses.description: This course delves into the art and science of social competence-knowing how to appropriately apply social skills in ways that meet the objective of the interaction, maintain self-esteem of both parties, improve the quality of the relationship, maintain a balance of power between the actors, and respect interpersonal human rights.  Students will obtain practical skills that will allow them to better "see" others in their fulness-while also being "seen" themselves.

courses.title: Sociological Explorations
courses.description: This course is designed to introduce students to the sociology major and provide them professional preparation for continuing in scholarship development and their respective sociology careers.  Topics will include: recognizing marketable sociology skills and how they be used to help others, research, career opportunities, graduate school, CVs, senior thesis and internships, and the sociological perspective.  Emphasis will be placed on the evaluation of social science research, including methods, logic, synthesizing findings, application, and sociological writing. No mathematical or statistical background is required.
courses.corequisiteText: Completed or concurrently enrolled in: ; SOC111 - Introduction to Sociology (3)

courses.title: Student Special Topics
courses.description: This is a student lead course that covers a variety of sociological topics as determined by the department.  It is not counted toward program credits, but should be taken for interest in the topic.

courses.title: Sociological Theory
courses.description: Students will examine the major theoretical perspectives of sociology and will learn how various sociological thinkers explain specific behaviors and phenomena. Through these explanations they will come to better understand why individuals, groups, institutions, and societies act and work as they do. In addition to discussing specific theoretical processes and concepts, students will also explore how theory fits into the general social scientific process. They should leave the class with a clear understanding of what theory is and how it can be (and has been) used to further our knowledge of the social world.
courses.corequisiteText: Completed or concurrently enrolled in: ; SOC230 - Sociological Explorations (3)

courses.title: Sociology of the Family
courses.description: This course will help students understand how social forces influence American family life, including their own family changes. We will learn about the history of marriage and family life in America as well as current trends in dating, cohabitation, marriage, childbearing, divorce, and repartnering.  We will also seek to understand differences in family structure and how those differences impact adults and children.

courses.title: Race and Ethnic Relations
courses.description: This course examines the historical social construction of race in the U.S., the development of racist practices by individuals and institutions and the consequences of those practices, especially the persistence of racial inequality. We will examine U.S. racial/ethnic groups, including whites, as well as the intersections of race with other inequalities such as class and gender.

courses.title: Research Methods
courses.description: How do we critically evaluate research and evidence? Where can we find reliable information? This course provides students with essential tools to analyze various information sources and the skills to conduct their own research. Students will practice various research methods used by social scientists to answer research questions.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SOC230 - Sociological Explorations (3)
courses.corequisiteText: Completed or concurrently enrolled in: ; MATH221C - Social Science Statistics (3) ; SOC300 - Sociological Theory (3)

courses.title: Media and Popular Culture
courses.description: This course is designed to help students comprehend the connections between individuals, cultures, and media industries.  Emphasis is placed on understanding  popular culture through its creation, marketing, and consumption.  We will examine how social forces shape our music listening preferences and how our lives are influenced by popular media.

courses.title: Sociology of Religion
courses.description: Students will read and discuss different sociological perspectives related to religion as an institution.  They will look at explanations related to why people believe and what impact religion has on individuals and social life.  Students will analyze issues related to religious leadership, ritual and emotion, conversion, commitment, religious violence, and the fate of religion in the world.  This will help students to develop a better appreciation of others, and the unique roles religion has.

courses.title: Sociology of Mental Health
courses.description: The escalating rates of depression and anxiety in the US, with 1 in 4 adults facing a diagnosable mental health disorder, demand a deeper understanding of their underlying causes. Emphasizing the biopsychosocial model, which considers the interplay of biological, psychological, and social factors in mental health, students will explore recent research on the social causes of depression and anxiety. This exploration will include evidence-based practices that can improve mental health outcomes for both individuals and society. To gain further insight into the role of the social environment on mental health, students will learn how to conduct population-level research on ways the disease burden of mental illness may be reduced. Students will obtain practical knowledge regarding the social causes of mental illness and social strategies that can improve mental health outcomes, which will aid them professionally, in their homes, the Church, and communities.

courses.title: Social Stratification
courses.description: This course presents a sociological approach to the dilemma of power, economic and status differentiations in American society.

courses.title: Crime and Delinquency
courses.description: Why do people commit crime? This course explores the social forces behind crime and delinquency, from peer pressure to broken social systems. We'll dive into major criminological theories, real-world cases, and how the justice system responds. Students will give presentations on key topics, analyzing crime from a variety of perspectives. Expect engaging discussions, interactive learning, and a fresh look at crime in society!

courses.title: Direct Study
courses.description: In this course students will develop a further understanding of special interest topics in sociology.  Students will choose a sociological topic that is approved by the instructor.

courses.title: Sociological Analysis
courses.description:
In an increasingly data-driven world, the ability to manage, analyze, and interpret survey data is an essential skill for understanding and addressing complex social phenomena. This course, "Sociological Analysis”, provides students with a comprehensive, hands-on introduction to the practical applications of survey data analysis within a sociological framework. Students will learn the fundamentals of data management, statistical analysis, and interpretation, highlighting the importance of clearly communicating research findings.

This course emphasizes the development of practical skills that enable students to draw meaningful insights into social patterns, trends, and relationships from large, publicly available, secondary survey data. Students will explore a variety of analytical techniques, including descriptive statistics, bivariate statistics, and regression analysis, learning how to apply these techniques to real-world sociological research questions. Through analyzing existing datasets and completing applied projects, students will gain proficiency in managing large datasets, identifying relevant variables, conducting statistical analyses, and interpreting results within the context of sociological thought.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; MATH221C - Social Science Statistics (3)
courses.corequisiteText: Completed or concurrently enrolled in: ; SOC340 - Research Methods (3)

courses.title: Demography
courses.description: How do birth and death rates shape the future of a country? What happens when people start living much longer--or stop having children? How do migration, urbanization, and divorce impact families, communities, and the environment? This course explores how fertility, mortality, and population changes influence the world around us. Using secondary data, students will create a demographic profile for a real-life client. By the end of the course, students will understand how population trends shape both daily life and global events.

courses.title: The City, Conflict, and Social Change
courses.description: This course examines the city through a societally based lens. Students will learn about the evolution of cities throughout history, the impact of the industrial city on social life, ways urban design can help solve social problems (crime, traffic, social isolation, deviance, group conflicts), and how to identify solutions in working toward a city that is beneficial to all. In short, students learn how understanding the relationship between the city and social life can help make the world a better place.

courses.title: Special Topics in Sociology
courses.description: The department will determine special areas of study that will benefit the Sociology students in giving them additional preparation related to the field. Term of enrollment, credit and other details will be arranged by the department and the instructor.

courses.title: Senior Thesis
courses.description: This is a graduate level workshop for students who have a strong interest in research or who are preparing to attend graduate or professional school. In previous courses students should have learned all the tools necessary to produce excellent research. During this workshop, they will apply what they have learned at the highest level possible in the time given.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SOC400 - Sociological Analysis (3)

courses.title: Senior Internship in Sociology
courses.description:
Internship credits are exempt from tuition charges. However, an administrative fee equal to one credit hour at the current rate of tuition will be charged for an internship course. The fee is in addition to any tuition charges for other classes. Fees are charged independently of tuition and are not subject to the 12-credit tuition cap.

This course is intended to help sociology majors apply their formal education to “real world” work experience.  An internship will provide students with an opportunity to apply sociological concepts and theories while gaining valuable work experience.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SOC300 - Sociological Theory (3)

courses.title: Beginning Spanish I
courses.description: This course is for beginners with less than two years of high school Spanish.  Emphasis is on basic language skills of listening speaking, reading, and writing. Not appropriate for Spanish-speaking returned missionaries.

courses.title: Beginning Spanish II
courses.description: In this course emphasis is on basic language skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Not appropriate for Spanish-speaking returned missionaries
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPAN101 - Beginning Spanish I (4)

courses.title: Intermediate Spanish
courses.description: This course is a review and continuation of first year grammar, conversation, reading, and writing. Not appropriate for Spanish-speaking returned missionaries
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPAN102 - Beginning Spanish II (4)

courses.title: Readings in Hispanic Literature
courses.description: This course is an introduction to literature in Spanish: prose, poetry, drama. Not appropriate for Spanish-speaking returned missionaries.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPAN201 - Intermediate Spanish (4)

courses.title: Advanced Spanish Grammar I
courses.description: This course involves intensive study and practice with grammar, vocabulary, listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Entry level for native speakers, returned missionaries, and other advanced non-natives.

courses.title: Advanced Spanish Grammar II
courses.description: This course involves continued intensive study and practice with grammar, vocabulary, listening, speaking, reading, and writing for advanced speakers.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take 1 of the following courses: ; SPAN202 - Readings in Hispanic Literature (3) ; SPAN302 - Advanced Spanish Grammar I (3)

courses.title: Spanish Phonetics and Conversation
courses.description: This courses involves the Spanish sound system, underlying concepts of speech production and pronunciation.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take 1 of the following courses: ; SPAN202 - Readings in Hispanic Literature (3) ; SPAN302 - Advanced Spanish Grammar I (3)

courses.title: Introduction to Literary Analysis
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the major concepts, problems, issues, and practices of literary study in Spanish.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPAN321 - Advanced Spanish Grammar II (3)

courses.title: Hispanic Civilization and Culture
courses.description: This course involves the study of major issues, periods, and themes in the culture of Spain and Spanish America.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take 1 of the following courses: ; SPAN202 - Readings in Hispanic Literature (3) ; SPAN302 - Advanced Spanish Grammar I (3)

courses.title: Spanish Teaching Methods
courses.description:
In this course students will develop Spanish teaching skills and theories of second language acquisition.
Spanish Education Majors, Spanish Education Minors, and French Education Minors are required to complete an 8-hour experience for this course.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take 1 of the following courses: ; SPAN202 - Readings in Hispanic Literature (3) ; SPAN302 - Advanced Spanish Grammar I (3)

courses.title: Spanish Teaching Methods II
courses.description: The second of two courses on foreign language teaching methodology. This course emphasizes technology, cross-cultural and linguistic assessment, and classroom management.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take 1 of the following courses: ; SPAN202 - Readings in Hispanic Literature (3) ; SPAN302 - Advanced Spanish Grammar I (3)

courses.title: Masterpieces of Spanish Literature
courses.description: In this course students will study literary masterpieces of Spain.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPAN339 - Introduction to Literary Analysis (3)

courses.title: Masterpieces Spanish-American Literature
courses.description: In this course students will study literary masterpieces of Spanish America.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPAN339 - Introduction to Literary Analysis (3)

courses.title: Spanish Special Topics
courses.description: In this course literary, cultural, linguistic, or pedagogical topics may be discussed.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPAN321 - Advanced Spanish Grammar II (3)

courses.title: Independent Study in Spanish
courses.description: This course consists of independent projects monitored through periodic conferences and assessments by instructor.

courses.title: Spanish Teaching Practicum
courses.description: This course consists of supervised practice and development of Spanish teaching skills.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPAN377 - Spanish Teaching Methods (3) ; SPAN378 - Spanish Teaching Methods II (3)

courses.title: Assistive Technology
courses.description: This course is an introduction to assistive technology devices and services when working with students with disabilities in a public education environment.  The legal basis for assistive technology will be the foundational structure for exploring the use of assistive technology for assessment; the use of assistive technology for access; the use of assistive technology to support academic learning; and the use of assistive technology as an augmentative communication tool.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPED424 - Assessment and Evaluation (4)

courses.title: Exceptional Students: P-Grade 6
courses.description: This course will emphasize the types and developmental patterns of specific exceptionalities (including giftedness and poverty), addressing risk factors, etiology, characteristics, and classification of common disabilities.  Focus will also be on legal issues, parent/student rights, responsibilities of teachers, both general education and special education, quality teaching for ALL students, including intervention strategies, accommodations, and the use of community resources to meet children's individual needs.  Child maltreatment, including legal requirements, is introduced.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take 1 of the following courses: ; CHILD150 - Foundations of Early Childhood (3) ; EDCOR200 - Teaching as a Profession (2)

courses.title: Legal Issues
courses.description: An in-depth examination of special education law, including the policies and procedures implemented in public education. IDEA, Section 504 and ADA will be compared and applied to the school setting. The six basic principles of disability law and their implementation in special education are covered, including student disciplinary procedures, bullying, extended school year, etc. Teacher candidates will learn their role in ensuring that legal rights and responsibilities of students with disabilities, their parents, and teachers are protected.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; EDCOR340 - Diverse and Exceptional Students (3)

courses.title: Evidence-Based Practices
courses.description: This course is an introduction to evidence-based practices related to the field of special education. Types of educational research will be examined along with legal policies and criteria for identifying evidence-based practices. Teacher candidates will be exposed to current evidence-based practices such as Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS), Response to Intervention(RtI), and Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) and their implementation in the educational environment.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPED310 - Exceptional Students: P-Grade 6 (3)

courses.title: Social Behavior Strategies for Students with Disabilities
courses.description: Prospective special education teachers will explore methods, strategies, and accommodations for teaching students with emotional and behavioral disorders. Cognitive, social, and learning characteristics of students with emotional and behavioral disorders will be identified. Teacher candidates focus on aspects of a positive classroom environment and supporting students in crisis. Using assessment, specific plans, and de-escalation techniques, students explore interventions to help children learn at the highest possible level within their abilities.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPED424 - Assessment and Evaluation (4)

courses.title: Special Education Focused Practicum
courses.description: Prospective special education teachers will receive practical, first-hand experience working with a special education teacher in a public-school setting. Opportunities for engaging in both formal and informal assessment activities, designing individualized curriculum, accommodating the general education curriculum, monitoring student progress, and collaborating with other professionals and families will be embedded within the practicum experience. A weekly two-hour seminar will serve as the forum in which teacher candidates can address challenges and concerns while sharing experiences, expertise and successes. SPED 410 teacher candidates will provide instruction to special education students at designated schools in the Jefferson, Madison, Idaho Falls and Sugar-Salem School Districts.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; ED245 - Early Field Practicum (2)

courses.title: Autism Spectrum Disorders
courses.description: Designed as an elective course for students desiring a more in-depth knowledge and understanding of autism spectrum disorders.  Topics include the history, diagnostic criteria, current research and theories, family impact, and researched-based strategies/interventions for working with individuals with autism.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take 1 of the following courses: ; SPED310 - Exceptional Students: P-Grade 6 (3) ; EDCOR340 - Diverse and Exceptional Students (3)

courses.title: Assessment and Evaluation
courses.description: In this course teacher candidates are introduced to and required to apply test and measurement theory, including the selection, administration, and interpretation of assessment tools. The course includes assessment strategies spanning the continuum from informal to formal. Child progress monitoring and program evaluation are also included. Teacher candidates use assessment data to inform instruction and make decisions in mock MDT and IEP meetings. Concepts are applied via video case studies and direct assessment of children.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; ED345 - Idaho Comprehensive Literacy #2 (3)

courses.title: Senior Practicum
courses.description: This course is designed for ECSE and SPED K12 majors. Students will transform from students to teachers of children. They will serve in a public school classroom two full days and attend two-hour seminars each week. Students will design and implement a unit of instruction, teach and manage a class, complete special education tasks, set weekly goals, and reflect on personal and professional growth. These experiences facilitate the process of becoming an educator; the more students engage, the more meaningful and effective this process becomes. Students will create and build relationships with classmates, a mentor teacher, university instructors, and the children in their class. Relationships are enhanced as students strive to have the Spirit and help others feel the Savior’s light and love. Students will put into practice all they’ve learned in previous courses and experiences to teach in the Savior’s way.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPED424 - Assessment and Evaluation (4)

courses.title: Students with Severe Disabilities
courses.description: Prospective special education teachers will be introduced to the medical, cognitive, motor, and communication needs of students with severe disabilities. The requirements and procedures for alternative assessment will be taught and implemented. Emphasis will be placed on designing curriculum including technology for students with severe disabilities. Legal and ethical considerations for providing educational services for students with severe disabilities will be explored.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SPED380 - Legal Issues (3)

courses.title: Social Work Freshmen Seminar
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the social work faculty. Students will learn about the social work professional program, build relationships with others who are also working on their social work degree, and learn to streamline their social work education to become a social work professional as soon as possible.

courses.title: Introduction to Social Work
courses.description: This course will explore what it means to be a social worker and uncover the numerous ways we can make a difference. Students will discover the values and ethics that guide social work practice, reveal the history and social policies that shape the profession, and learn how social work advocates for social and economic justice, and human rights. We will use hands-on activities and discussions to enrich learning and bring these concepts to life. This course highlights ways the social work profession is dedicated to creating positive change in the lives of individuals, families, and the community.

courses.title: Social Work Research Methods
courses.description: This course seeks to develop basic capabilities in the following areas: consume and understand research; understand quantitative and qualitative research designs; formulate social work problems; collect, organize and analyze data; write and present research.  This knowledge base will lead to the ability to incorporate evidence based practice into a social work generalist approach.  Practical uses for research include informing policy, promoting social change, improving clinical practice, and enhancing program delivery.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; MATH221C - Social Science Statistics (3)

courses.title: Social Work Practice I - Individuals
courses.description: This course will introduce, explore, and blend knowledge, values, ethics, and skills used by social workers.  Social Work practice using the generalist method e.g., relationship identifying issues, problems, resources, assessment, intervention, evaluation, and termination with a diverse client population will be covered.

courses.title: Social Work Practice II - Groups
courses.description: The basic knowledge and skills necessary to lead and participate effectively in small groups will be taught. Students will participate in small group experiences.

courses.title: Social Work Practice III - Community
courses.description: This class prepares students to intervene with communities on the macro level.  Students will develop skills in community assessment, leadership, advocacy and community organization from the perspective of social work generalist practice.

courses.title: Human Behavior in Social Environment
courses.description: This course investigates multiple theories of human behavior and person-in-environment that equip students with a sound theoretical understanding when working with clients on the individual, family, group, organization, and community levels. In addition, this course explores how knowledge of human development across the lifespan and cultural responsiveness influence the appropriate application of theory during the engagement, assessment, and intervention phases of the generalist social work practice model.

courses.title: Internship Seminar I
courses.description: Field education in social work is consistent with the mission goals and objectives of the BYU-Idaho social work program. The student will be placed in social service/social work agencies and get actual experience in social work. The goal is to integrate academic knowledge with actual experience (empirical and practice based knowledge). This experience will help the student to reinforce identification with the purposes, values and ethics of the social work profession, promote professional competence, and students will be evaluated on the basis of consistency with program objectives. This is the capstone experience in baccalaureate social work education, students will work 500 hours in their field placements. Thus, only those students who are in their last year of baccalaureate social work education and who have completed the requisite course work and who are deemed prepared by the social work field coordinator shall be allowed to take SW 397, 398, and SW 497 & 498.  The first and second field internships/practicums at BYU-Idaho are integral parts of our generalist's social work education.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SW362 - Social Work Practice I - Individuals (3) ; SW364 - Social Work Practice II - Groups (3) ; SW365 - Social Work Practice III - Community (3) ; SW367 - Human Behavior in Social Environment (3) ; SW400 - Social Work Values and Ethics (3)

courses.title: Internship I
courses.description:
Internship credits are exempt from tuition charges. However, an administrative fee equal to one credit hour at the current rate of tuition will be charged for an internship course. The fee is in addition to any tuition charges for other classes. Fees are charged independently of tuition and are not subject to the 12-credit tuition cap.

This course is a supervised field experience in a social service agency. Supervision by a social worker is needed. Students will gain experience and intervention to apply knowledge, values, and practice skills in actual social work settings. Must be concurrently enrolled in SW 397 to be eligible to be enrolled in this course. This capstone experience in baccalaureate social work education is the first internship and students will work 250 hours in their field placements.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SW362 - Social Work Practice I - Individuals (3) ; SW364 - Social Work Practice II - Groups (3) ; SW365 - Social Work Practice III - Community (3) ; SW367 - Human Behavior in Social Environment (3) ; SW400 - Social Work Values and Ethics (3)

courses.title: Social Work Values and Ethics
courses.description: An overview of values and principles of ethical decision making for social workers using the National Association of Social Workers Code of Ethics as a backdrop.  Students will have the opportunity to become aware of personal values, the values of the social work profession, and to discuss various ethical dilemmas and their effect on agencies, clients, and social work practice.  Students will learn that social work values and ethics are woven into the fabric of generalist social work practice with all populations.

courses.title: Child Welfare Services
courses.description: This course is planned and organized to acquaint students with the role of the generalist social work practitioner in the field of child welfare.  An overview of public and private programs that provide services to children is provided.  These services include counseling, adoptions, foster care, residential care, school-based services, home-based services, court services, and daycare services.  Also addressed are social problems that impact children, particularly those who are disadvantaged because of disability, racism, sexism and poverty.

courses.title: Intervention Diverse Clients
courses.description: This course develops competency for generalist social work practice with diverse clients. It includes improving self-awareness, gaining knowledge of racial/ethnic groups, and conducting multi-level social work practice based on the client's cultural reality.

courses.title: Social Work in Community Mental Health
courses.description: This course studies the bio-psycho-social aspects of emotional maladjustments.  The history of community mental health will be studied as well as various aspects of assessment, social causations, treatment, and preventions of mental illness.  Using the generalist social work method, the role of the baccalaureate social worker in community and behavioral mental health is explored.

courses.title: Social Welfare Policy
courses.description: This course will help a student develop an understanding of the history of Social Work and social welfare services and the role of policy delivery in Social Work practice.  The student will understand the role of policy in service delivery and practice and attainment of individual and social well being. Knowledge and skills to understand and analyze organizational, local, state, national, and international issues in social welfare policy and social service delivery will be developed.  Students will also develop skills to use policy practice to influence, formulate, and advocate for policy consistent with Social Work values.

courses.title: Special Topics
courses.description: The department will determine special areas of study that will benefit social work students in giving them additional preparation related to the field.  Term of enrollment, credit and other details will be arranged by the department and the instructor.

courses.title: Internship II
courses.description:
Internship credits are exempt from tuition charges. However, an administrative fee equal to one credit hour at the current rate of tuition will be charged for an internship course. The fee is in addition to any tuition charges for other classes. Fees are charged independently of tuition and are not subject to the 12-credit tuition cap.

The goal is to integrate academic knowledge with actual experience (empirical and practice based knowledge). This second semester internship experience will help the student to reinforce identification with the purposes, values and ethics of the social work profession, promote professional competence, and students will be evaluated on the basis of consistency with program objectives. This capstone experience in baccalaureate social work education is the second internship and students will work 250 hours in their field placements.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; SW397 - Internship Seminar I (2) ; SW398 - Internship I (3)

courses.title: Career and Orientation
courses.description: This course introduces the theatre arts major to the department's philosophy, mission, resources, and guidelines. The course helps students explore possible emphasis and career options and helps students identify their interests, needs, and skills in the area of theatre. It will give focus to what theatre is and how it relates within the historical and cultural framework of the church.

courses.title: Introduction to Theatre
courses.description: Through non-performance-based collaboration, students will identify and appreciate the critical perceptions and internal workings of theatre, as well as the people who take theatrical production from the page to the stage. Whether theatre is a career path or a passionate hobby, students will explore various aspects of the theatrical world through an introductory lens.

courses.title: Dramatic Structure and Analysis
courses.description: This course studies the fundamentals of play analysis and dramatic theory. Students will learn to critically analyze a script to uncover how identified elements and aspects work together to support and strengthen its message. This will be accomplished through class demonstration and discussion, class exercise, small group activities, play reading, and through attending live performances. It is recommended to be completed during the first year of study.

courses.title: Introduction to Film Art and Analysis
courses.description: This course develops analytical skills for understanding motion pictures as an art form, with attention to their history, theory, and aesthetics.

courses.title: Introduction to Technical Theatre
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the theory and practice of scenery construction, painting, lighting, and rigging. Laboratory experience includes actual participation working backstage in university productions. Technical Theatre minors must enroll in this course during the first semester of their freshman year.

courses.title: Voice Diction
courses.description: This course teaches vocal production skills for the stage.  Emphasis is given to learning and developing basic vocal skills such as flexibility, projection, placement, and articulation in preparation for voice interpretation.  A beginning study of the International Phonetic Alphabet and its application in good speech is also covered.

courses.title: Acting I
courses.description: This course studies and applies basic voice and movement to the art of acting. Students use improvisation, concentration, and characterization to develop scripted and non-scripted performances.

courses.title: Stage Makeup
courses.description: This course explores the theory and practice of theatrical makeup.

courses.title: Technical Theatre Practicum
courses.description: This course involves work in a specific area of technical theatre on a university production.

courses.title: Theatre Design Fundamentals
courses.description: This course will help students develop the skills to: determine the objectives of dramatic works as they read critically, investigate and analyze the script, and effectively research the world of the play, cultivate curiosity to empathetically observe others and their feelings, thoughts and surroundings, develop a vocabulary of design elements, succinctly articulate their developing design ideas orally, visually and in writing, prepare to create purposeful, effective and unified theatrical designs that tell a story, collaborate and communicate with others, document their development.

courses.title: Acting II
courses.description: This is an experiential course which will help the student investigate, select, and prepare audition material appropriate to a variety of audition situations. This course includes exercises in handling cold readings, writing resumes, and discussions in the business end of acting. Students will learn to look at auditions from the casting director's point of view and engage in discussion and feedback.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; TA121 - Voice Diction (2) ; TA123 - Acting I (3)

courses.title: Stage Dialects
courses.description: This course involves an intense study of the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) and its direct application and use with dialects in performance.  Students acquire an understanding of several dialects for stage work, with mastery in some dialects.  A major focus of the course is understanding and mastering the International Phonetic Alphabet.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; TA121 - Voice Diction (2)

courses.title: Unarmed Stage Combat
courses.description: This movement course will strengthen the performance skills of actors, singers, and dancers by refining kinesthetic awareness and nonverbal expressiveness.  This course is designed to help each student become more aware of his/her body's movement and expressive potential.  Unarmed Stage combat is one of the most used disciplines in stage combat and will be applied to the work of actors and directors.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; TA123 - Acting I (3)

courses.title: Improvisational Theatre
courses.description: This course explores various components and applications of improvisational theatre. Participants will be textually and experientially trained in both dramatic and comedic improvisation as an art form, including an exploration in both short-form improvisation game and long-form improvisation scene work.

courses.title: Theatre Sound Design
courses.description: This course deals specifically with the theatre sound design experience, including the basics of working collaboratively with the director and other designers for an imaginative, appropriate sound design, as well as the basics of research, recording, editing, and playback of sounds and music, the basics of microphone use and equipment care, and other topics relating to the role of the theatre sound designer.
courses.prerequisiteText: Take the following course(s): ; TA217 - Theatre Design Fundamentals (2)

courses.title: Theatre Properties
courses.description: This course follows both a cognitive and a kinesthetic model.
